children.text: In November 1922, a step was found in the
Valley of the Kings
The find was by workers on Howard Carter's excavation. The spot was in a corner of the valley many believed exhausted. Yet the step led to a sealed tomb.

Weeks later, Carter and his patron Lord Carnarvon peered through a small hole in the sealed entrance. Candle light reached gilded couches, boxes, chariots, guardian figures, and vessels. Carnarvon asked "can you see anything?" and Carter is said to have answered "yes, wonderful things."
That moment made Tutankhamun the most famous pharaoh in the world.
Why this discovery was special
Tutankhamun wasn't a great king in life.

A young 18th Dynasty king, he ascended after Akhenaten's religious reform and was involved in restoring the traditional religious order centred on Amun. His reign was short; he died in his late teens.
Tutankhamun's fame doesn't come from his lifetime achievements. It comes from his tomb surviving nearly intact.

Many royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings were looted from antiquity. Large important tombs were known early and stripped. Tutankhamun's tomb was small and the entrance was hidden by later work and debris, so it survived not fully lost.
The tomb shows traces of ancient intrusion. Even so, most contents remained. A royal tomb with this much grave goods being found in the modern archaeological era was unprecedented.
Howard Carter's search
Howard Carter originally came to Egypt as a painter.

Beginning by copying wall paintings, through long involvement in Theban west-bank sites, he became an excavator who knew the Valley of the Kings very well. He believed Tutankhamun's tomb hadn't yet been found.
Small objects bearing the king's name and burial-related fragments supported the belief. Previous excavators thought no major find remained in the valley; Carter didn't accept it.
With Lord Carnarvon's funding, Carter searched for years. With no results, talk of stopping arose. As a final chance, examining part of the valley again, the step was found.
The discovery was dramatic; the work that followed was longer and more mundane. Opening a tomb isn't the end. Recording, photographing, conserving, and removing contents took roughly ten years.
What was inside
Tutankhamun's tomb KV62 isn't a large tomb.

In a relatively small space — antechamber, burial chamber, treasury, and annex — over five thousand items were packed. Gilded furniture, chariots, bows, staves, clothes, boxes, statues, ritual items, shabtis, jewellery, coffins, shrines, canopic containers. Things deemed needed for a young king to head to the afterworld, densely remained.
Most famous is the golden mask. The mask covering Tutankhamun's face became an image symbolising ancient Egypt. The tomb's value isn't only the mask.
Small chairs, sandals, clothes, games, hunting gear convey aspects close to the king's life. Showing the king as a sacred being and a young man actually alive.
The arrangement of items in the tomb is very important for knowing the practice of ancient burial. Recording which items lay where and how rooms were used greatly raised archaeological value.
Records that changed archaeology
What matters in Carter's excavation isn't only the discovery's lavishness.
Before removing items, he photographed, numbered, recorded positions, and noted condition. Standard practice in current archaeology; very thorough for the time.
Thanks to this recording, KV62 is not simply "a tomb where treasure came out" but a tomb from which the burial state can be reconstructed. Beyond items, the relation of items and space was preserved.
Tutankhamun's tomb showed the move of archaeology from treasure hunt to record-based discipline, in a form easy for the public to see.
Egypt and the question of ownership
1922, when Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered, was important for Egyptian politics too.
Egypt was moving from British influence toward formal independence; who owned antiquities wasn't only an academic matter. The era of foreign excavators taking finds abroad was changing.
Tutankhamun's grave goods remained in Egypt. An event strongly showing the idea that Egyptian cultural heritage belongs to Egypt.
Today, Tutankhamun's major grave goods can be seen at the Grand Egyptian Museum in
Giza
. The king's mummy remains at KV62 in the Valley of the Kings. So understanding Tutankhamun involves both the Giza museum and the
Luxor
tomb.
On the curse
"The pharaoh's curse" attaches to Tutankhamun's tomb.
One trigger was Lord Carnarvon's death soon after opening. Newspapers made it large, and the story spread that a curse fell on those who disturbed the tomb.
No famous curse phrase was written in the tomb. Carnarvon's death is thought to have been from infection. Before antibiotics spread, such infections could be fatal.
The curse story is less archaeology and more a product of media and popular culture. Old tombs do hold real health dangers — dust, mould, poor ventilation. Not supernatural curses.
The curse isn't central to understanding Tutankhamun's discovery. What's central is how the tomb survived, how it was recorded, and how the world received it.
Worldwide Egypt fever
Tutankhamun's discovery created worldwide Egypt fever.
1920s fashion, jewellery, architecture, film, and advertising took in Egyptian-style design. Golden mask, cobra, wings, geometric pattern, and pharaoh imagery tied with Art Deco aesthetics.

The fever also relied on press power then. The discovery was treated large in papers, reaching world publics through photos and stories. The archaeological field became, for the first time, a massive event in popular media.
Tutankhamun's fame wasn't made by ancient greatness alone. The era of discovery, the way of reporting, the visual strength of the gold grave goods, and the story "almost intact royal tomb" layered.
Where to see today
The tomb itself is at KV62 in the Valley of the Kings on Luxor's west bank.
KV62 is a small tomb in the valley. Wall paintings are mainly in the burial chamber; expecting the grandeur of Seti I's or Ramesses V/VI's tombs, it can feel unexpected.

KV62's value isn't size. The meaning is that this is the tomb Carter found, and where Tutankhamun's mummy still rests. Visiting the Valley of the Kings, even after treasures moved to the museum, this place has worth.

For grave goods, the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza is the centre. Official ticketing includes Tutankhamun Galleries access. Before visiting, confirm hours, ticket, and display scope on the official site.
Cairo
's old Egyptian Museum lets you feel the history of Egyptology from before Tutankhamun. For the main Tutankhamun collection, the Grand Egyptian Museum is now the natural axis.
Including in the itinerary
To follow Tutankhamun's story properly, split into two places.
In Luxor, see KV62 in the Valley of the Kings. With time, also see KV17 and KV9 — larger, more decorated tombs — to feel KV62's smallness and specialness clearly.
In Giza, see grave goods at the Grand Egyptian Museum. Beyond the golden mask, furniture, chariots, jewellery, ritual items, and near-daily items show how broad the tomb's contents were.
Order works either way. See items at the museum then the tomb and the space's smallness stays. See the tomb then the museum and the surprise at what fit in that narrow room rises.
Why it still matters
Tutankhamun wasn't Egypt's strongest king.

His tomb showed what ancient Egyptian royal burial was, in an unprecedented form. Beyond gold's beauty, furniture, clothes, ritual, daily items, and preparation for the afterworld remained in one tomb.

This discovery affected archaeology, museums, cultural property ownership, popular culture, and tourism. Tutankhamun became a historical presence less through life's achievements and more through the moment of being found.
It was also chance. The tomb being small. The entrance being hidden. Carter not giving up. 20th-century media telling the world. All layered.
Seeing Tutankhamun's tomb isn't only seeing ancient Egypt.
It is also seeing how the modern era discovered, recorded, owned, and imagined the ancient.

deck: In 1922 Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings. The story, why it mattered, and where to see the tomb and treasures today.
